title: The Hypertext Transfer Protocol Status Code 308 (Permanent Redirect)
summary: Specifies the HTTP status code 308 (Permanent Redirect). It is like 301 but does not allow the request method to change when the client follows the redirect. It was published as experimental and was replaced by RFC 7538.

eli5.summary: When a shop moves to a new address, a sign tells you the new place, and you should keep doing the same thing there. This was a trial version of that sign and was replaced by a later one.

subtitle: A redirection status code that preserves the HTTP request method.

tldr.problem: HTTP 301 allows clients to change POST requests to GET when following a redirect, but some applications need the method to stay the same when resources move permanently.
tldr.mechanism: HTTP status code 308 (Permanent Redirect) signals a permanent move like 301, but explicitly forbids method changes, keeping POST as POST.
tldr.outcome: RFC 7238 was published as experimental in 2014 to fill this gap, and was later replaced by RFC 7538 with the same specification.

facts.label: Method preservation
facts.value: POST and other methods are not changed

today: RFC 7238 was published as Experimental in June 2014. It was later superseded by RFC 7538, which carries the same specification as a Standard status code instead of Experimental.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
HTTP uses status codes to tell clients where a resource has moved. The protocol defines three redirect codes for permanent and temporary moves, organized by whether they allow the client to change the request method from POST to GET.

Status code 301 (Moved Permanently) allows method changes. Code 307 (Temporary Redirect) does not. HTTP was missing a permanent variant of 307, which this specification provides as status code 308.
sections.eli5: The web has a few different 'moved' signals. This one says 'gone forever, but keep doing exactly what you were doing.'

sections.title: The 308 Permanent Redirect Status Code
sections.content:
The 308 status code indicates that the target resource has been assigned a new permanent URI and any future references should use the new address. Clients with link editing capabilities ought to automatically re-link references from the old URI to the new one.

A server SHOULD generate a Location header field in the response containing the preferred URI for the new permanent location. The response is cacheable by default unless otherwise indicated by cache controls. Unlike 301, a 308 response must not change a POST request into a GET request.
sections.eli5: The server sends back a 308 and says 'the real address is here' (in the Location header). Your browser must resend the same kind of request (POST stays POST) to the new address.

sections.title: Deployment Considerations
sections.content:
Because 308 was new when RFC 7238 was published, clients that did not yet understand it would treat it like the generic 300 Multiple Choices response. Servers therefore could not rely on automatic redirection, limiting early use to situations where the server had high confidence in client support or where fallback to 300 semantics was acceptable.

The RFC advises against 'User-Agent Sniffing'—varying the status code based on browser type—as this makes code hard to maintain and debug. HTML <meta refresh> directives can serve as a fallback when browser clients encounter the code.
sections.eli5: When this code was new, many browsers did not understand it, so servers had to be careful about using it. They could also put a refresh link in the HTML page as a backup.

sections.title: Security and IANA Considerations
sections.content:
All security considerations that apply to HTTP redirects apply to 308 as well (see RFC 7231 Section 9). The redirection mechanism itself does not introduce new security risks beyond those inherent to any redirect.

IANA registered status code 308 in the Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) Status Code Registry under the name 'Permanent Redirect' with a reference to this specification.
sections.eli5: Status code 308 follows the same safety rules as other HTTP redirects. IANA (the organization that manages protocol numbers) officially added it to the list of valid HTTP status codes.
